title: India's Startup Funding Fell 9% in the First Half of 2026. But Five New Unicorns Say That's Not the Whole Story.
excerpt: AI investment exploded 317%, Bengaluru captured more than half of all capital, and 75% of listed startups are now profitable — the ecosystem is maturing, not shrinking
body:
The headline number looks like a slowdown: Indian startups raised $5.2 billion in the first half of 2026, down 9% from $5.7 billion in the same period last year.

But zoom in, and the story is more complicated — and arguably more encouraging — than the top line suggests.

The number of deals actually increased 7% year-over-year to 501. More than 1,100 investors actively backed startups during the half. Five companies crossed the billion-dollar valuation threshold to become unicorns. And AI funding didn't just grow — it erupted, surging 317% to $676 million.

The money didn't disappear. It got more selective.

## The AI Explosion

If there's a single defining trend in Indian venture capital right now, it's artificial intelligence. AI startups raised $676 million across 57 deals in H1 2026 — a 317% year-over-year jump in funding and a near-doubling of deal volume.

The biggest contributor was Sarvam AI, which raised $234 million in a round that vaulted it to unicorn status. But the momentum extends well beyond a single mega-round. The government's IndiaAI Mission has strengthened investor confidence by backing compute infrastructure and indigenous AI development, and global investors are rotating from distribution-moat businesses toward technology-moat companies.

"First, the global AI infrastructure buildout has created real enterprise demand," said Vikram Gupta, managing partner at IvyCap Ventures. "Second, investors are moving away from businesses where the moat is distribution towards companies where the moat is technology."

Deeptech more broadly also performed well, with advanced hardware and technology startups securing $365 million — up 17% — across 66 deals.



> **""First, the global AI infrastructure buildout has created real enterprise demand," said Vikram Gupta, managing partner at IvyCap Ventures."**


## The Five New Unicorns

India minted five new unicorns in H1 2026, matching last year's pace despite the tighter funding environment: **Sarvam** (AI), **JusPay** (payments infrastructure), **KreditBee** (digital lending), **Square Yards** (proptech), and **Skyroot** (space technology).

The diversity of the list is notable. It spans AI, fintech, real estate, and aerospace — a signal that India's unicorn factory is no longer just a consumer-internet story. Skyroot, in particular, represents the emergence of a credible private space sector in India, while JusPay's inclusion highlights the depth of India's payments infrastructure stack.

## Where the Money Went — and Didn't

The capital shift is visible in the stage breakdown. Late-stage funding plunged 27% to $2.2 billion, with only four rounds exceeding $100 million — CRED ($900 million), KreditBee ($280 million), Rapido ($240 million), and Sarvam ($234 million). The median late-stage check size collapsed 68% to $10 million.

Growth-stage startups, by contrast, emerged as the biggest winners. Series A and B funding climbed 15% to $2.3 billion, with deal volume surging 33% to 190 transactions. Investors are diversifying across a wider base of startups rather than concentrating bets on a handful of unicorn candidates.

Early-stage funding bucked the broader moderation entirely. Seed-stage startups raised $478 million, an 18% increase, with a steady median ticket size of $1 million.

"From where we stand as early-stage investors, we haven't seen a slowdown," said Kannan Sitaram, cofounder and partner at Fireside Ventures. "We're continuing to see strong entrepreneurship, new founding teams and plenty of capital flowing into early-stage consumer companies."

## Bengaluru's Dominance

Geographically, Bengaluru is pulling away from the pack. The city attracted $2.7 billion across 165 deals — more than half of the country's total. CRED, Rapido, Sarvam, and KreditBee all call Bengaluru home, and the city has become the undisputed centre for AI, fintech, and deeptech investment.

Delhi NCR held second place despite a 39% correction to $917 million. Mumbai ranked third at $587 million.

## M&A Over IPOs

The exit landscape is shifting. IPO activity remained subdued due to market volatility — fundraising through public listings plunged 89% in the June quarter. But mergers and acquisitions stepped in: Indian startups recorded 52 M&A deals in H1 2026, broadly in line with last year and significantly higher than the second half of 2025.

Investors now expect secondary buyouts and strategic M&A to account for the majority of startup exits over the next two years, with IPOs resuming only after growth-stage companies demonstrate sustained profitability. The market is watching large listings like NSE and Jio Platforms, both of which are expected to file in the second half.

One encouraging datapoint: 75% of India's listed startups are now profitable, indicating that the public market is rewarding companies that balance growth with operational discipline. India's New Age Tech Index outperformed the Nifty 50 by 8.5 percentage points despite declining market capitalisation.

## What Comes Next

The second half of 2026 will likely be shaped by three forces: the global AI buildout continuing to pull capital into Indian AI companies, a potential reopening of the IPO window if markets stabilise, and the Indian government's increasing focus on semiconductors and deeptech through initiatives like the India Semiconductor Mission.

For diaspora investors — many of whom are LPs in India-focused venture funds or active angels — the message is clear: the era of spray-and-pray is over. The ecosystem is rewarding founders who can build technology moats, demonstrate unit economics, and scale without burning cash. That's not a slowdown. That's growing up.
